a.pick: lost on the moor, as he says

why: A man who has lost his way on the moor would not know that a stable-boy sleeps alone in this stable every night.

a.pick: strayed loose on the moor

why: The most remarkable horse in England, loose on a thinly peopled moor, would have been seen within two days, and it has not been.

a.pick: with the gypsies

why: A large reward is offered and the gypsies themselves are searching for the horse. Hiding it would gain them nothing.

a.pick: gypsies

why: The gypsies are on the alert for the reward. Thieves of so famous a horse could not sell it, and they could not claim the reward either.

a.pick: they received the horse from Simpson by arrangement

why: With a large reward out and the gypsies watching for the horse, taking it in from Simpson would be a great risk for no gain.

a.pick: the_stranger

why: Hunter was across the stable unloosing the dog when the stranger leaned in. He did not see any drugging; he only concluded it afterwards.

a.pick: a drug for the boy's supper

why: Simpson says the paper was a ten-pound note, and one was found in his purse. A note is just what a tout offers a lad for a tip.

a.pick: to drug the lad and take the horse

why: If the folded paper was a ten-pound bribe still in his purse, the one sign that he meant to drug the lad falls away.

a.pick: simpson

why: The dog had been set on this very stranger that evening. Yet when the door was opened and the horse taken out, nothing woke the lads overhead.

a.pick: simpson

why: The horse's track runs alone from the hollow until a man joins it near Mapleton. Nobody led it away from the killing, as the police say Simpson did.

a.pick: silas_brown

why: The man's track joins the horse's only near Mapleton. Whoever met it there did not bring it out of the stable or the hollow.

a.pick: one person took the horse and killed the trainer who got in the way

why: If a thief killed the trainer while leading the horse off, the horse would not have crossed the moor alone afterwards.

a.pick: to carry him off and hide him

why: A man carrying the horse off would have led it away from the hollow, but it went off alone.

a.pick: simpson

why: Straker's knife was bloody to the handle, yet Simpson has no wound on him.

a.pick: an assailant's

why: The only suspect bears no wound, so the blood on the knife may not be an attacker's at all.

a.pick: an assailant's blade

why: The man accused has no knife, and the only very sharp blade at the scene was in Straker's own hand.

a.pick: silas_brown

why: Brown came upon the horse wandering loose on the moor at dawn, by chance. That does not fit a man who had been in the hollow with it in the night.

a.pick: he threw it off to fight

why: The coat was laid across the bush, calmly, not flung aside in a struggle.

a.pick: to defend himself

why: A man snatching a weapon would not cap its tip, and in a sudden fight he would not stop to take the cork off. Yet the cork lay by the body.

a.pick: to see that all was well with the horses

why: A man checking the stables would be at the stables. Straker was found a quarter-mile out on the moor, in a hollow, with the horse.

a.pick: to watch for the stranger's return

why: A man watching for a tout in the dark has no use for a candle stub and a fine surgeon's blade.

a.pick: by habit, or to light his pipe

why: A match was struck down in the hollow where he died. A light was wanted there, out of sight, not just for his pipe.

a.pick: a friend of Straker's, as Mrs. Straker says

why: The friend's bill was in Straker's own pocket and his letters came to Straker's house, and Mrs. Straker never had such a dress.

a.pick: mrs_straker

why: She says she never had such a costly costume.
A trainer who is merely comfortably off is carrying a bill with a twenty-two-guinea costume on it.

a.pick: at the bottom of a pit or old mine on the moor

why: Holmes firmly advises keeping the horse entered for Tuesday. He expects it alive and able to run.

a.pick: dead, the body not yet found

why: No one keeps a dead horse in the entries. Holmes expects Silver Blaze to run.

a.pick: taken a long way off

why: The horse's track ends at the gates of Mapleton, two miles from King's Pyland.

a.pick: led away over ground that takes no prints

why: The prints show up again in the wet ground, and they are the horse's alone; nobody led it.

a.pick: back towards King's Pyland

why: Silver Blaze's own shoe fits a fresh track in the hollow on the line towards Mapleton.

a.pick: simpson

why: The man's track went in at Mapleton's gates. Simpson lodges at the villas to the north and has no known link with Mapleton.

a.pick: no part in it

why: The track of the horse and the man leading it ends at the gates of Brown's own stables.

a.pick: he went that way for some other reason, such as to keep out of sight

why: He came back the same way and took the horse in at Mapleton's gates, not on to anywhere hidden.

a.pick: back at King's Pyland

why: Holmes insisted the horse stay entered for the Cup, so the place that matters is the race.

a.pick: a horse runs in his colours, but not Silver Blaze

why: Holmes asked whether the Colonel would know his horse when he saw him. He expected the horse not to look like itself.

a.pick: another horse run in the Colonel's colours

why: The horse was hidden by an old horse-faker who asked whether to 'change it'. Markings can be covered, so having no white hair proves little.

a.pick: an ordinary ailment, of no account

why: Holmes was looking for something amiss with the sheep and calls the lameness a singular epidemic worth the Inspector's attention.
